en.title: Mass Communication: The Whole Course
en.short: What mass communication covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the field is
sections.text:
Mass communication is the study and practice of producing messages for large, scattered audiences through organised media. These media include newspapers, radio, television, film, websites, apps and social platforms. The field asks who makes messages, why they make them, how those messages reach people, and what happens next.

It matters because most people learn about elections, health, prices and distant events through media. A society’s media can inform and connect people. They can also mislead and divide people. Graduates work as reporters, editors, broadcasters, public relations officers, advertising staff, researchers and development workers.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
A BSc usually takes four years in Nigeria. Ghana, Kenya and South Africa have their own degree lengths and titles. In the Nigerian polytechnic system, the ND and HND each usually take two years, with industrial attachment between them. The NUC guides university programmes and the NBTE guides polytechnic programmes.

First-year work usually covers communication concepts, media history, writing and basic reporting. Later years add specialist practice, law, ethics, management, research methods and a final project. Attachment to a newsroom, station or agency is common.

Programme structures change. Reports from 2020 onward say that Nigeria’s NUC approved seven separate degrees alongside the general one: Journalism and Media Studies, Public Relations, Advertising, Broadcasting, Film and Multimedia Studies, Development Communication Studies, and Information and Media Studies. Universities need accreditation for each. Reports also say that the NBTE split the polytechnic HND into Journalism and Media Studies, Strategic Communication and Media Studies, and Film and Multimedia Production. Check what your own institution offers.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The course starts with concepts and models of communication, then normative press theories. Next comes the history of the media, in the world and in Africa. News values, news writing and reporting give you the core skills of journalism.

The core years build on this foundation. You study theories of media effects, editing, broadcast journalism, public relations, advertising, and digital and social media. You also study media law, with attention to Nigeria and to other legal systems, followed by ethics, media management, photojournalism, film and multimedia, and development communication.

At master’s level, the work becomes more critical and research-based. Students examine media and society, political communication and advanced research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Practise as well as read. Write news stories to a word limit. Record a radio script and time it. Edit a classmate’s copy. Skills improve through feedback and repetition.

Link each theory to a real example. Learn the name, the date, the main claim and one criticism. When you read a report, ask who the sources are and what is missing.

Learn the law and the regulators of your own country, and know that other countries differ. Laws, regulators and court decisions change, so check the current official source before relying on any rule. Facts about the media landscape go out of date quickly. Always give a date when you state one, such as the number of stations or the audience of a platform.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often treat a model as a fact. A model simplifies, and each has limits. Many also present American or British theory as universal without asking whether it fits their own society.

In writing, common faults are burying the main fact, adding your own opinion to a news story, and failing to attribute claims. Some students confuse public relations with advertising, or libel with slander. Others confuse Nigeria’s two bodies with the initials NBC. The old Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation was a broadcaster, and today’s National Broadcasting Commission is a regulator.

In research, a common fault is a sample that cannot support the conclusion. Another is a claim about media effects based only on counting content. Content analysis shows what was published. It does not show what audiences thought or did.

keyPoints: Mass communication studies organised messages sent to large, scattered audiences.
Courses combine theory, practical skills, law, ethics and research.
Media law and regulators differ by country, so always name the country.
Give a date with any fact about the media landscape.
A model or theory simplifies reality, so learn its limits as well as its claim.

en.title: What Is Mass Communication?
en.short: Levels of communication, the features of mass communication and the functions of the media.

sections.heading: Levels of communication
sections.text:
Communication is the process of creating and sharing meaning through symbols such as words, images and gestures. Scholars often describe several levels. Intrapersonal communication happens inside one person, as when you think through a decision. Interpersonal communication takes place between a few people. Group communication involves a small group, and public communication is one speaker addressing an audience.

Mass communication differs from these levels in scale and organisation. A media organisation produces messages that reach a large, scattered and mixed audience, usually at the same time or within a short period.

sections.heading: Main features
sections.text:
Traditional mass communication has several features. The sender is usually an organisation, not a single person. It needs technology to carry the message. The audience is large and mostly unknown to the sender. Feedback is limited and delayed. A radio listener in Kumasi cannot stop a presenter to ask a question, although a phone-in or a text message may reach the studio later.

Digital media have blurred these features. One person with a phone can reach thousands of people, and audiences can reply at once. Because of this, many scholars now speak of mediated or networked communication as well.

sections.heading: Functions of the media
sections.text:
Harold Lasswell (1948) named three social functions. Surveillance means watching the environment and reporting on it, such as giving flood warnings. Correlation means explaining events and helping society respond, as in editorials and analysis. Transmission means passing culture and values to new generations. Charles Wright (1960) added entertainment.

Later writers add mobilisation, which means encouraging action, such as joining a vaccination campaign. Commercial media also have an economic function, because they connect advertisers with buyers.

Functions can also go wrong. Wright called harmful effects dysfunctions. A report on a disease outbreak may warn people, but a careless report may cause panic.

keyPoints: Common levels are intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, public and mass communication.
Mass communication is organised, depends on technology and reaches a large, scattered audience.
Lasswell named surveillance, correlation and transmission of culture.
Charles Wright added entertainment and discussed dysfunctions.
Digital media have blurred the line between sender and audience.

en.title: Models of Communication
en.short: Linear, interactive and mass models from Lasswell, Shannon and Weaver, Schramm, Berlo and others.

sections.heading: Why we use models
sections.text:
A model is a simplified picture of a process. It helps us name the parts of communication and see where things go wrong. No model is complete, and each reflects the concerns of its time.

The main terms are these. The source creates the message. Encoding turns an idea into symbols. The channel carries the message. Decoding is how the receiver interprets it. Feedback is the response that returns to the source. Noise is anything that interferes with the message.

sections.heading: Linear models
sections.text:
Lasswell (1948) offered a verbal model: who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect. It gives a useful plan for study, but it has no feedback and it assumes that messages always have effects.

Shannon and Weaver (1949) described a source, transmitter, channel, receiver and destination, with noise affecting the signal. They were working on telephone and signal problems, so the model is technical. Communication scholars later extended the idea of noise. Static on a radio is physical noise, and an unfamiliar word is semantic noise.

Berlo (1960) proposed the SMCR model: source, message, channel, receiver. He stressed that skills, attitudes, knowledge, social position and culture affect both source and receiver.

sections.heading: Interactive and mass models
sections.text:
Schramm (1954) showed that people both encode and decode. He argued that communication works only where the fields of experience of sender and receiver overlap. A health message full of medical terms may fail with a farmer in Kano because of this gap, not because of a faulty signal.

Westley and MacLean (1957) adapted these ideas to mass media. They placed a media organisation between events and audiences. That organisation selects what to pass on, which relates to gatekeeping.

These models still treat communication mainly as transmission. Later work, including Stuart Hall’s encoding and decoding, gives audiences a more active role in making meaning.

keyPoints: A model simplifies a process and always leaves something out.
Lasswell: who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect.
Shannon and Weaver introduced noise in a technical, linear model.
Berlo’s SMCR stands for source, message, channel, receiver.
Schramm stressed overlapping fields of experience.
Westley and MacLean placed media organisations between events and audiences.

en.title: Normative Theories of the Press
en.short: Authoritarian, libertarian, social responsibility and other views of how media ought to work.

sections.heading: What normative means
sections.text:
A normative theory says how the media ought to operate in a society. It does not describe what the media actually do, and it does not measure their effects. Such theories matter because they shape laws, regulators and professional codes.

The classic text is Four Theories of the Press by Siebert, Peterson and Schramm (1956).

sections.heading: The four original theories
sections.text:
Authoritarian theory holds that the media should serve those in power. Control may come through licences, censorship and punishment.

Libertarian theory, also called free press theory, draws on thinkers such as John Milton and John Stuart Mill. It holds that people can find truth through open debate, sometimes called a marketplace of ideas. Government control should be minimal.

Social responsibility theory accepts press freedom but adds duties to society, such as accuracy and fair representation of groups. It is linked to the Hutchins Commission in the United States (1947).

Soviet theory held that the media should serve the working class and the state’s socialist goals. Ownership was by the state or party.

sections.heading: Later additions
sections.text: Denis McQuail added two further ideas. Development media theory holds that, in countries building their economies and institutions, media should support national development goals. Critics warn that governments can use this idea to justify control. Democratic-participant theory favours small, community-based media and the right of citizens to take part. Community radio is a clear example.

sections.heading: Limits and newer approaches
sections.text:
The 1956 book reflects the Cold War, and critics such as Nerone and others (1995) have challenged it. Real systems also mix these ideas. A country’s constitution may promise press freedom while other laws restrict it.

Hallin and Mancini (2004) took a more descriptive approach. They compared media systems in Western Europe and North America, and named three models: liberal, democratic corporatist and polarised pluralist. Their study was not designed for Africa, so apply it to African systems with care.

keyPoints: Normative theories state how media ought to work, not what they actually do.
The original four are authoritarian, libertarian, social responsibility and Soviet.
McQuail added development and democratic-participant theories.
Development media theory can be used to justify state control, so it is debated.
Hallin and Mancini compare media systems and name three Western models.

en.title: History of the Media in the World
en.short: From early news sheets and the printing press to radio, television and the internet.

sections.heading: From writing to print
sections.text:
Societies shared news long before printing, through town criers, drums, messengers and marketplaces. Ancient Rome posted public notices called the Acta Diurna. Printing developed early in China and Korea. In Europe, Johannes Gutenberg’s movable-type press of about 1450 made it cheaper to produce many copies, which helped spread literacy and new ideas.

One of the earliest printed newspapers in Europe appeared in Strasbourg in 1605. Governments often licensed or censored printers, and arguments for press freedom grew in response.

sections.heading: The mass press
sections.text: The nineteenth century brought a true mass press. Steam-powered printing, rising literacy and advertising made papers cheap. In 1833 the New York Sun sold for one cent, which began the American penny press. The telegraph sped up news, and agencies such as AP (1846) and Reuters (1851) sold news to many papers. In the 1890s, sensational and exaggerated American reporting became known as yellow journalism. A reaction against it helped strengthen ideas of professional, objective reporting.

sections.heading: Radio, television and film
sections.text: Guglielmo Marconi developed wireless telegraphy in the 1890s. Regular radio broadcasting began around 1920, and the BBC started in 1922 as a company and became a public corporation in 1927. Film became a mass entertainment form in the early twentieth century. Television services grew from the 1930s and spread widely after 1945. Communication satellites from the 1960s and cable news from the 1980s allowed live coverage across borders.

sections.heading: The digital era
sections.text: ARPANET, a forerunner of the internet, began in the United States in 1969. Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989. Since then, smartphones, search engines and social platforms have changed how news is found and paid for. Each new medium has tended to change older media instead of replacing them. Radio survived television, for example, and it changed its role.

keyPoints: Gutenberg’s press of about 1450 made mass copying cheaper in Europe, though printing began earlier in Asia.
The penny press (1833) built a mass audience paid for largely by advertising.
Agencies such as AP and Reuters grew with the telegraph.
Yellow journalism in the 1890s helped provoke calls for professional standards.
The web was proposed in 1989, twenty years after ARPANET began.
New media usually change older media instead of replacing them.

en.title: History of the Media in Africa
en.short: Traditional communication, the colonial and nationalist press, broadcasting and the 1990s opening.
keywords: history of the press in Africa

sections.heading: Before and during early print
sections.text:
African societies had rich systems of communication before print. These included talking drums, town criers, griots and masquerades. Many scholars call these oramedia or traditional media, and they still work in development campaigns.

The earliest printing came through colonial and missionary contact. Mauritius had a French-run paper in 1773. Official gazettes followed in the Cape from about 1800, in Sierra Leone soon after, and on the Gold Coast in 1822 with the Royal Gold Coast Gazette. Henry Townsend, a missionary, started Iwe Irohin in Yoruba at Abeokuta in 1859. It is widely taught as Nigeria’s first newspaper. Claims about firsts in the early African press are often debated, and sources differ on some exact dates.

sections.heading: The nationalist press
sections.text: Educated Africans soon started their own papers. In South Africa, Imvo Zabantsundu began in 1884. In Lagos, The Anglo-African began in 1863, and John Payne Jackson’s Lagos Weekly Record began in 1890 or 1891. In Kenya, Jomo Kenyatta edited the Kikuyu-language Muigwithania from 1928. Nnamdi Azikiwe founded the West African Pilot in Lagos in 1937. Papers of this kind questioned colonial rule and helped build national movements.

sections.heading: Broadcasting
sections.text:
Colonial governments introduced radio, partly to relay the BBC. Lagos had a wired relay service in the 1930s, with sources giving 1933 or 1935. The Gold Coast began Station ZOY in 1935. Nigeria’s WNTV in Ibadan began in October 1959 and was described as the first television service in tropical Africa. Ghana began television in 1965. South Africa delayed it until 1976.

In Nigeria, the NTA name dates from 1977 and FRCN from 1978.

sections.heading: Control and opening
sections.text: After independence, many governments kept tight control of broadcasting, and some restricted the press. In the 1990s, political change opened the sector in many countries. The Windhoek Declaration (1991), from a UNESCO-supported meeting, called for a free, independent and pluralistic African press. Nigeria’s 1992 decree allowed private broadcasting, and Raypower radio began commercial broadcasts in 1994.

keyPoints: Traditional media such as talking drums and town criers came before print and remain in use.
Iwe Irohin (1859, Abeokuta) is widely taught as Nigeria’s first newspaper.
The nationalist press helped build movements against colonial rule.
WNTV Ibadan (1959) was described as the first TV service in tropical Africa.
The Windhoek Declaration of 1991 called for a free and pluralistic African press.
Nigeria opened broadcasting to private owners through a 1992 decree.

en.title: What Makes News: News Values and Gatekeeping
en.short: How editors decide what counts as news, including news values, gatekeeping and bias.

sections.heading: Defining news
sections.text: News is a report of a recent event or newly found information that interests or affects an audience. No definition is perfect. The same event may be front-page news in Enugu and may not appear at all in Nairobi. News is therefore selected and shaped by people and institutions, and it is not a mirror of the world.

sections.heading: Common news values
sections.text:
News values are the qualities that make a story likely to be chosen. Textbooks commonly list these:
Timeliness: it happened recently.
Proximity: it happened near the audience, or it feels close to them.
Prominence: it involves well-known people or bodies.
Consequence or impact: it affects many people.
Conflict: it involves a dispute or a contest.
Human interest: it touches the emotions.
Novelty: it is unusual.

A fuel price rise scores high on impact, for example, while a rescued child scores high on human interest.

sections.heading: Research on selection
sections.text:
Galtung and Ruge (1965) studied how foreign crises were reported in Norwegian newspapers. They named factors such as negativity, elite nations and elite people, and unexpectedness. Their work helps explain why poorer regions may appear in world news mainly during disasters. Harcup and O’Neill (2001, updated 2017) tested and revised such lists, adding factors such as shareability.

David Manning White (1950) applied Kurt Lewin’s term gatekeeping to a US wire editor, whom he called Mr. Gates. White stressed personal choice. Later research shows that deadlines, budgets, routines, ownership, advertisers, and now audience data and algorithms, also affect selection.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: News values describe common practice. They do not prove that a story is important. A focus on conflict and elites can leave out slow problems such as poor sanitation, and it can leave out rural people and women. A good journalist knows these habits and questions them.

keyPoints: News is selected and shaped, so it does not simply mirror events.
Common values are timeliness, proximity, prominence, impact, conflict, human interest and novelty.
Galtung and Ruge (1965) gave a classic list of foreign news factors.
White (1950) applied gatekeeping to news selection.
Routines, ownership, advertisers and algorithms also affect what appears.

en.title: News Writing: Leads, Structure and Style
en.short: How to write a news story, covering the five Ws and H, leads, the inverted pyramid and attribution.

sections.heading: The lead
sections.text:
Hard news reports recent events directly. Its core questions are the five Ws and H: who, what, when, where, why and how. The opening sentence is called the lead or intro. It gives the most important fact, usually in about 25 to 35 words, and it answers the questions that matter most for this story.

Here is an invented example: “Twelve traders were injured on Tuesday when a fire swept through Karu Market, the Federal Capital Territory’s fire service said.” The event comes first, and the source is named. A weak lead would begin: “The fire service held a press briefing on Tuesday.”

sections.heading: The inverted pyramid
sections.text:
The inverted pyramid places facts in order of importance, with the most important first. This helps readers who stop early, and it helps editors who need to cut from the bottom.

A simple plan is this:
Lead: the main fact.
Second paragraph: more detail or the source.
Quote: a person’s direct words.
Background: what led to this event.
Other details: less important facts.

Features and some online stories use other structures, such as a narrative opening. The inverted pyramid is a tool, not a rule for all writing.

sections.heading: Attribution and style
sections.text:
Attribution means telling readers where information came from. Attribute any claim that is not an established fact. “Said” is usually the safest verb, because “claimed” or “admitted” can suggest a judgement. Use direct quotes for strong or personal words, and paraphrase dull official language.

Keep the writer’s opinion out of hard news. Prefer short sentences, active verbs and plain words. Explain terms such as “inflation” when the audience may not know them. Follow your organisation’s house style for numbers, names and titles.

Check names, figures, dates and places before filing. One wrong figure can damage a story’s credibility, and it may also cause legal problems.

keyPoints: The lead gives the most important fact, usually in about 25 to 35 words.
The inverted pyramid orders facts from most to least important.
Attribute any claim that is not an established fact.
“Said” is usually the most neutral attribution verb.
Keep personal opinion out of hard news.
Check names, figures, dates and places before filing.

en.title: Reporting: Sources, Interviews and Verification
en.short: Finding stories, using sources, interviewing, checking facts and covering a beat.

sections.heading: Finding stories and sources
sections.text:
Reporters find stories through beats, which are regular areas of coverage such as courts or health. They also use public records, press releases, tips and community contacts.

Primary sources have direct knowledge, such as a witness or an original document. Secondary sources report what others said. A press release is a starting point, not a finished story. Always ask who benefits if the claim is believed.

Seek more than one source and include the people affected. Give anyone accused of wrongdoing a fair chance to respond before publishing.

sections.heading: Interviewing
sections.text:
Before an interview, research the person and the topic. Prepare questions, and ask the most important ones early. Open questions begin with how or why, and they bring explanation. Closed questions confirm a precise fact. Listen carefully and follow up instead of simply reading your list.

Agree on the terms of the interview. Terms such as “on the record”, “off the record” and “on background” can mean different things in different newsrooms, so settle what they mean with the source first. Use accurate notes or a recording, and follow your country’s rules on recording and consent.

sections.heading: Verification and investigation
sections.text:
Verification is the process of checking whether information is true. Compare claims with documents and independent sources. If a figure seems surprising, work it out yourself. If a report says a budget rose from ₦20 million to ₦25 million, the rise is ₦5 million, or 5 ÷ 20 = 25%.

Investigative reporting uncovers matters that someone wishes to keep hidden, usually over a long period. It relies on records and careful checking, and it also needs legal advice. Right to information laws, such as Nigeria’s Freedom of Information Act 2011 and Ghana’s Right to Information Act 2019, can help.

Anonymous sources need care. Use them only when there is no other way, and ask how the source knows. Keep any promise of confidentiality that you make.

keyPoints: A beat is a regular area of coverage, such as courts or health.
A press release is a starting point that must be checked.
Give anyone accused of wrongdoing a fair chance to respond.
Open questions bring explanation, and closed questions confirm facts.
Settle the terms of an interview with the source first.
Use anonymous sources only with care and with a clear reason.

en.title: Theories of Media Effects and Audiences
en.short: How thinking about media power moved from strong effects to agenda setting, framing and active audiences.

sections.heading: From strong to limited effects
sections.text:
Early thinking, often called the hypodermic needle or magic bullet idea, assumed that media messages strongly and directly affect a passive audience. Historians note that few scholars stated it in such a simple form, so treat it as a label for early fears.

Lazarsfeld, Berelson and Gaudet studied voters in Erie County, Ohio, in the 1940 US election (The People’s Choice, 1944). They found that personal contacts often mattered more than the media. Katz and Lazarsfeld (1955) developed the two-step flow: ideas may pass from media to opinion leaders, and then to others. Klapper (1960) summed up the limited effects view.

sections.heading: Cognitive and long-term effects
sections.text:
Later work looked at subtler effects. McCombs and Shaw (1972), studying voters in Chapel Hill during the 1968 US election, found that issues stressed by the media were the issues voters saw as important. This is agenda setting. The media may not tell people what to think, but they may influence what people think about.

Framing goes further. A frame is the angle that defines an issue. Fuel subsidies could be framed as help for the poor or as a cost to the budget.

Gerbner’s cultivation theory, from the 1960s and 1970s, argues that heavy, long-term television viewing shapes beliefs about social reality. Noelle-Neumann’s spiral of silence (1974) argues that people who believe their view is a minority may stay silent, which makes that view seem weaker still.

sections.heading: Active audiences
sections.text:
Uses and gratifications (Katz, Blumler and Gurevitch, 1974) asks what people do with the media. People may seek information, identity, company or escape. Critics say the approach can neglect media power and depends on what people report about themselves.

Most scholars now accept that effects depend on the person, the message and the context. Results from the United States may not transfer to other societies. Where a platform’s algorithm personalises content, researchers also ask whether a shared media agenda still exists.

keyPoints: The hypodermic needle idea assumed direct effects on passive audiences.
The two-step flow gives a role to opinion leaders.
Agenda setting concerns what people think about (McCombs and Shaw, 1972).
Framing concerns how an issue is defined.
Cultivation concerns long-term effects of heavy viewing.
Uses and gratifications asks what people do with the media.

en.title: Editing and Newspaper Production
en.short: Copy editing, headlines, the editorial chain, page design and online editing.

sections.heading: What editors do
sections.text:
Editing improves a story before it reaches the audience. It checks accuracy, fairness, clarity, length and legal risk. A typical newspaper chain runs from reporter to section editor, then to copy editor or sub-editor, then to the editor. Titles and structures differ between organisations.

A structural edit, sometimes called substantive editing, asks whether the story is complete, balanced and in the right order. Copy editing fixes grammar, style, facts and flow. Proofreading is the final check of the finished page for errors.

sections.heading: Copy-editing practice
sections.text:
Read the whole story first. Ask whether the lead carries the main fact. Check every name, title, date and figure against the source material. Add up totals. If a report says 300 of 1,200 applicants passed, the rate is 300 ÷ 1,200 = 25%.

Mark any statement that could be defamatory or could prejudice a court case, and refer it to a senior editor or a lawyer. Follow the house style, which is the organisation’s own rules on spelling, numbers and titles. Respect the writer’s meaning. If a change alters a fact, check with the reporter.

sections.heading: Headlines and design
sections.text:
A headline gives the main point in a few words. It should be accurate and supported by the story, and it usually uses a strong, active verb in the present tense. “Kisumu council cuts market fees”, an invented example, is clear. A misleading headline can damage trust even when the story below it is correct.

Page design arranges stories, images and white space to show importance and to help reading. Designers use a grid, a clear hierarchy of type, and a dominant image or story. Writing captions is often part of the editing process.

sections.heading: Editing for digital
sections.text: Online editors also write search-friendly headlines, add links, choose images, and update stories as facts change. Speed adds pressure, but checks must remain. Correct errors openly, and state what changed. Avoid clickbait, which means a headline that promises more than the story delivers.

keyPoints: Editing checks accuracy, fairness, clarity, length and legal risk.
Structural editing, copy editing and proofreading are different stages.
House style sets an organisation’s rules on spelling, numbers and titles.
A headline must be supported by the story beneath it.
Online editing adds links and updates, and errors should be corrected openly.

en.title: Broadcast Journalism: Radio and Television
en.short: Writing for the ear, bulletins, packages, shot types and how broadcasting systems are organised.

sections.heading: Systems of broadcasting
sections.text: Broadcasters are often grouped as public service or state, commercial and community stations. Each has a different source of funds and a different purpose. Radio remains important in much of Africa, because receivers are cheap, it reaches people who cannot read, and it can use local languages. Many stations now also stream online. Check current figures, as the sector changes quickly.

sections.heading: Writing for the ear
sections.text:
A listener cannot read a sentence again, so broadcast copy must be clear at first hearing. Write short sentences with one idea each. Put attribution first: “Police say two people have died”, and not “Two people have died, police say.” Round numbers where exact figures do not matter, saying “nearly two million” for 1,985,000. Spell difficult names phonetically for the newsreader.

Timing matters. Many newsreaders read about 150 to 180 words a minute, though speed varies by language and station. At 160 words a minute, a 30-second story is about 160 × 0.5 = 80 words.

sections.heading: Formats and production
sections.text:
Common radio formats include the copy story, read by the presenter, and the voicer, in which a reporter speaks. A package combines the reporter’s voice with clips from people interviewed, called actuality or sound bites. A vox pop is a set of short opinions from the public. It shows a range of views, but it does not measure public opinion.

Television adds pictures. Shot sizes include the wide shot, medium shot and close-up. A piece to camera shows the reporter speaking at the scene. Script and pictures should support each other. Producers plan a bulletin through a running order, usually with the most important story first. Live broadcasts carry a higher risk because errors and defamatory remarks cannot be removed before they go out.

sections.heading: Standards
sections.text: Most regulators expect accuracy and fairness. Some systems also require impartiality, especially at elections. Rules differ by country. Nigeria’s National Broadcasting Commission, the UK’s Ofcom and South Africa’s ICASA each apply their own codes and rules.

keyPoints: Stations are commonly public or state, commercial or community.
Broadcast copy must make sense at first hearing, so use short sentences.
Attribution usually comes first in broadcast writing.
At 160 words a minute, 30 seconds is about 80 words.
A vox pop shows a range of views, but it is not a poll.
A package combines the reporter’s voice with clips from interviews.

en.title: Public Relations
en.short: What PR is, Grunig and Hunt’s four models, the RACE process, crisis work and professional bodies.

sections.heading: What public relations is
sections.text:
Public relations (PR) is the planned management of communication between an organisation and its publics, in order to build understanding and protect reputation. Publics are groups with an interest in the organisation, such as staff, customers, regulators and neighbours. PR differs from advertising. An organisation pays for advertising and controls its wording, while PR often seeks coverage that journalists choose to give, which is known as earned media.

Good PR is honest. It is not the same as spin, which means presenting facts in a misleading way.

sections.heading: Models and process
sections.text:
Grunig and Hunt (1984) described four models. Press agentry seeks attention, sometimes with little regard for full truth. Public information gives accurate information in one direction. Two-way asymmetric uses research to persuade publics. Two-way symmetric uses dialogue, and both sides may change. Critics say that the symmetric ideal may understate differences of power.

The RACE formula, linked to John Marston (1963), gives a planning process: research, action planning, communication and evaluation. Evaluation should measure outcomes, such as changes in understanding or behaviour, as well as press cuttings.

sections.heading: Crisis communication
sections.text:
A crisis is a serious event that threatens people or reputation. Prepare a plan and a trained spokesperson before one happens. When a crisis occurs, put people’s safety first, respond quickly, and tell the truth about what is known and unknown.

Suppose an invented water company in Mombasa finds contaminated supply. It should warn customers at once, give safe alternatives, explain its actions and update people regularly. Delay and denial often make the damage worse.

sections.heading: The profession
sections.text: In Nigeria, the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations began in 1963 as the Public Relations Association of Nigeria, and took its present name in 1972. A 1990 decree gave it chartered status. In the UK, the Chartered Institute of Public Relations received its charter in 2005. Ghana and South Africa have their own institutes. Membership rules and codes differ by country, so check the current rules of the relevant body.

keyPoints: PR manages communication between an organisation and its publics.
Grunig and Hunt’s four models are press agentry, public information, two-way asymmetric and two-way symmetric.
RACE stands for research, action planning, communication and evaluation.
In a crisis, put safety first, respond quickly and tell the truth.
NIPR was chartered in Nigeria by a 1990 decree.

en.title: Advertising
en.short: How advertising works, AIDA, campaign planning, media buying sums and regulation in several countries.

sections.heading: What advertising is
sections.text:
Advertising is paid, identified communication from a sponsor, designed to persuade an audience about a product, service or idea. Product advertising sells goods. Corporate advertising builds an organisation’s image. Public service advertising promotes social goals such as road safety.

A common explanation of how adverts work is AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action. It helps writers, but buyers do not always follow these steps in order. Petty and Cacioppo’s elaboration likelihood model (1986) adds that people who care about a topic weigh arguments, while others respond more to cues such as an attractive presenter.

sections.heading: Planning a campaign
sections.text: A campaign usually moves through these steps: research, objectives, target audience, budget, message strategy, media plan, production and evaluation. An agency’s account team handles the client, its creative team writes and designs, and its media team buys space and time.

sections.heading: Media buying sums
sections.text:
Reach is the share of the target audience exposed at least once. Frequency is the average number of exposures among those reached. Gross rating points (GRPs) equal reach × frequency. If an advert reaches 40% of the audience an average of 3 times, it earns 40 × 3 = 120 GRPs.

CPM is the cost per thousand people reached. If a ₦450,000 slot reaches 300,000 people, CPM = ₦450,000 ÷ 300,000 × 1,000 = ₦1,500. Also consider whether the audience fits the product.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.text:
Advertising should be truthful and clearly recognisable as advertising. Paid promotion by online influencers raises the same issue of disclosure.

In Nigeria, the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON), formerly APCON, works under an Act of 2022. In November 2025, the Federal High Court in Lagos gave power over outdoor advertising to local government councils, while the same court in Lokoja upheld ARCON’s role. ARCON said it would appeal, so check the current position. In the UK, the Advertising Standards Authority applies the codes. In South Africa, the Advertising Regulatory Board handles complaints. In the US, the Federal Trade Commission acts against deceptive advertising.

keyPoints: Advertising is paid and identified, with a clear sponsor.
AIDA stands for attention, interest, desire, action.
GRPs = reach × frequency, so 40 × 3 = 120.
CPM is the cost per thousand people reached.
Regulators differ by country, such as ARCON in Nigeria and the ASA in the UK.
Paid promotion must be disclosed, including by online influencers.

en.title: Digital and Social Media
en.short: Convergence, platforms and algorithms, false information, online verification and data protection.

sections.heading: Convergence and new roles
sections.text:
Convergence means that once-separate media now share digital networks and devices. A single reporter may write text, record audio and shoot video for the same story. Henry Jenkins (2006) also stressed participation: audiences now create and share media themselves. Citizen journalism refers to news reporting by people who are not professional journalists. It can supply first images of an event, but those images still need checking.

Digital media can be interactive, rapid and global, and they can be kept and searched long after publication. Mobile phones are a major route to the internet in many African countries, though cost and coverage still create a digital divide between groups.

sections.heading: Platforms and algorithms
sections.text:
Platforms are services that host and distribute content made by others. Their algorithms are sets of rules that rank content, often using signals of attention such as shares and viewing time. This affects what audiences see, and it can favour emotional content.

Eli Pariser (2011) popularised the term filter bubble for the idea that personalisation narrows what people see. Researchers still debate how strong this effect is. Features and policies change often, so learn the principles and do not depend on one service.

sections.heading: False information and verification
sections.text:
Wardle and Derakhshan (2017) drew a useful distinction. Misinformation is false, but it is shared without intent to harm. Disinformation is false and is shared to cause harm. Malinformation is true information shared to cause harm, such as leaked private details.

To check online material, find the original source. Use reverse image search to see whether a picture is old. Check the date, the place and who gains from it. Compare with independent sources. Images, audio and video created by AI can look real, so treat them with extra care, and label such material honestly.

sections.heading: Privacy
sections.text: Personal data law applies to much digital work. Examples include Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023, Kenya’s Data Protection Act 2019, South Africa’s POPIA and the UK’s Data Protection Act 2018. Their exact rules differ.

keyPoints: Convergence means that media share digital networks and devices.
Algorithms rank content, and this affects what audiences see.
Misinformation lacks intent to harm, and disinformation is meant to harm.
Malinformation is true information shared to cause harm.
Verify online material by tracing its origin, date and place.
The digital divide means that access differs between groups.

en.title: Media Law: Core Principles Across Countries
en.short: Free expression, defamation, contempt and copyright in Ghana, Kenya, South Africa, the UK and the US.

sections.heading: Free expression and its limits
sections.text:
This summary is not legal advice. Laws change, so check the current official source.

Most constitutions and rights treaties protect expression, but usually allow limits for reasons such as reputation or public order. The First Amendment protects the press in the United States. Section 16 of South Africa’s Constitution and Articles 33 and 34 of Kenya’s Constitution protect expression and the media. Ghana’s 1992 Constitution gives media freedom its own chapter and creates the National Media Commission.

sections.heading: Defamation
sections.text:
Defamation is a false statement that harms a person’s reputation in the eyes of others. In many common law systems, libel is the permanent form, such as print, and slander is the spoken form. A claimant generally shows that defamatory words referred to them and reached a third person. Common defences include truth, fair comment and privilege, such as fair court reports.

Countries differ:
US: New York Times v Sullivan (1964) requires public officials to prove actual malice.
UK: the Defamation Act 2013 for England and Wales requires serious harm, and it sets out defences of truth, honest opinion and publication on a matter of public interest.
South Africa: National Media v Bogoshi (1998) allows the media a defence of reasonable publication.
Ghana: Parliament repealed criminal libel in 2001, though false news provisions remained.
Kenya: in Okuta v Attorney General (2017), the High Court held Penal Code criminal defamation unconstitutional. The prosecutor gave notice of appeal, but no appeal decision was found in 2026.

sections.heading: Contempt and copyright
sections.text:
Contempt of court includes reporting that may prejudice a case in progress. In the UK, the Contempt of Court Act 1981 applies strict rules. Many countries protect the identity of children and of victims of sexual offences.

Copyright protects original works, such as articles, photographs and music. It generally does not protect facts or ideas themselves. Limited use for news reporting may be allowed, but rules differ by country. A picture found online is not automatically free to use.

keyPoints: Freedom of expression is widely protected, but usually not without limits.
Libel is usually the permanent form of defamation, and slander the spoken form.
Sullivan (US, 1964) requires public officials to prove actual malice.
The UK’s Defamation Act 2013 includes a serious harm requirement.
Bogoshi (South Africa, 1998) created a reasonable publication defence for media.
Copyright protects original expression, not facts or ideas.

en.title: Media Law and Regulators in Nigeria
en.short: Nigeria’s Constitution, NBC, Press Council, NUJ, FOI Act, Cybercrimes Act and defamation rules.

sections.heading: The Constitution and access to information
sections.text:
This summary is not legal advice. Check current official sources. The position below is as reported up to November 2026.

Section 39 of the 1999 Constitution protects freedom of expression and the right to own media, with conditions for broadcasting. Under section 22, the press, radio and television shall be free to uphold the fundamental objectives and government accountability. Section 45 allows laws limiting some rights in certain interests.

The Freedom of Information Act 2011 gives a right to request public records, subject to exemptions. The Official Secrets Act restricts disclosure of classified material.

sections.heading: Regulators and professional bodies
sections.text:
The National Broadcasting Commission (NBC), set up by Decree 38 of 1992, regulates broadcasting and issues the Nigeria Broadcasting Code. A 2020 amendment raised the hate speech fine from ₦500,000 to ₦5 million, and it was disputed.

Federal High Court judgments in 2023 and 2024 held that the NBC cannot impose fines. Reports, based mainly on Media Rights Agenda, which brought both cases, say the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal against the 2023 judgment in April 2026. They say it struck out the appeal against the 2024 judgment in June 2026 because of a defective notice. In August 2026 the NBC sought leave to appeal afresh. No ruling was reported by November 2026.

The Nigerian Press Council, set up by Decree 85 of 1992, handles complaints about the press. The Federal High Court ruled against its Act in 2010, and the Court of Appeal reversed this in 2015. A Supreme Court appeal was reported pending in 2021, and no outcome was found. In 2023 the ECOWAS Court ordered amendments on journalists’ age and qualifications.

The Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), founded in 1955, is a union and not a government regulator.

sections.heading: Offences and other risks
sections.text:
Defamation can give rise to a civil claim, and the Criminal Code and Penal Code contain criminal defamation provisions. In Arthur Nwankwo v The State (1985), the Court of Appeal held sedition provisions inconsistent with the 1979 Constitution.

In 2020 and 2022 the ECOWAS Court found section 24 of the Cybercrimes Act 2015 incompatible with human rights treaties. A 2024 amendment narrowed it to pornographic messages and messages known to be false and sent to cause a breakdown of law and order or threaten life. The ECOWAS Court later dismissed a challenge to the new text, but critics say the risks remain. The Copyright Act 2022 and the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 also affect media work.

keyPoints: Section 39 of the 1999 Constitution protects expression, and section 45 allows some limits.
The NBC regulates broadcasting, and its power to fine has been challenged in court.
The Press Council handles complaints about the press.
The NUJ is a union founded in 1955, not a government regulator.
The FOI Act 2011 gives a right to request public records, with exemptions.
The Cybercrimes Act was amended in 2024, and its use remains debated.

en.title: Media Ethics
en.short: Ethical frameworks, professional codes, gratification, privacy and handling harm in reporting.
keywords: Code of Ethics for Nigerian Journalists

sections.heading: Law and ethics
sections.text:
Law sets what you may or may not do, and courts enforce it. Ethics asks what you ought to do, and it relies largely on conscience, codes and peer pressure. An act can be legal yet unethical, such as naming a private person’s family member without need.

Duty ethics, associated with Kant, says that some actions are right or wrong in themselves. Utilitarian thinking, associated with Mill, weighs outcomes for the greatest number. Aristotle’s golden mean looks for a reasonable middle course. African scholars such as Francis Kasoma (1996) have argued for an ethics rooted in community, sometimes called Afriethics.

sections.heading: Professional codes
sections.text: Most codes share key values: truth, independence, fairness and limiting harm. The Code of Ethics for Nigerian Journalists (1998) covers issues including accuracy, privacy, gratification, children and plagiarism. A revised code was reported adopted in 2022, so check which applies. The US Society of Professional Journalists’ code has four principles: seek truth and report it, minimise harm, act independently, and be accountable and transparent. Voluntary press bodies exist elsewhere, such as IPSO in the UK and the Press Council of South Africa.

sections.heading: Common dilemmas
sections.text:
Gratification means accepting gifts or money that may affect coverage. In Nigeria and Ghana, cash given to reporters at events is often discussed as brown envelope journalism. It damages independence, even when a journalist’s pay is low. A conflict of interest arises when a reporter’s personal or financial interests could affect a story, and it should be declared or avoided.

Privacy may give way to public interest, which is not the same as what the public finds interesting. A leader’s misuse of public money concerns the public interest, while a private illness may not. Reports on suicide, violence and children need special care, including avoiding details that identify a child.

Deception, such as hidden recording, should be a last resort, used only for serious matters and with senior approval. Plagiarism means presenting another person’s work as your own.

keyPoints: Law is enforced by courts, while ethics relies mainly on conscience and codes.
Duty, utilitarian and golden mean approaches can give different answers.
Common values are truth, independence, fairness and limiting harm.
Gratification and conflicts of interest damage independence.
Public interest differs from what the public finds interesting.
Use deception only as a last resort, for serious matters.

en.title: Media Management and Economics
en.short: Ownership, how media organisations earn money, newsroom structure and basic budgeting.

sections.heading: Ownership and structure
sections.text:
Media may be owned by the state, by private individuals or companies, by a public trust or by a community. Each form creates its own pressures. A state broadcaster may face pressure from government, and a private outlet may face pressure from owners and advertisers. A community station may lack funds. Concentration of ownership means that a few owners control many outlets, which can reduce diversity. Rules on this differ by country.

A typical organisation has editorial, commercial, technical and administrative departments. Many outlets try to separate editorial and commercial decisions, so that advertisers do not influence the news. Managers plan, organise, lead and control, as in other firms, but they also protect editorial independence.

sections.heading: Media economics
sections.text:
Robert Picard (1989) described media as operating in a dual product market. They sell content to audiences, and they sell audience attention to advertisers. Media goods also have high first-copy costs: producing the first copy of a programme costs a great deal, and extra copies cost little. Digital distribution makes this even stronger.

Common income sources include advertising, sales and subscriptions, sponsorship, public funding, licence fees, grants and events. Online advertising has moved much revenue away from traditional media to large platforms, so many newsrooms now seek several income sources, including reader support. These trends vary by country and by period, so use current and dated evidence.

sections.heading: A budgeting example
sections.text:
Break-even is the point at which revenue equals cost. Suppose an invented radio station in Kisumu has fixed costs of KSh 600,000 a month. Each advertising slot brings in KSh 4,000 and has a direct cost of KSh 1,000.

Each slot contributes KSh 4,000 − KSh 1,000 = KSh 3,000 to fixed costs.
Break-even = KSh 600,000 ÷ KSh 3,000 = 200 slots a month.

Managers also consider audience research, staff training, safety and legal risks. Cutting reporters may save money in the short term, but weak content can reduce audience and income later.

keyPoints: Media may be state, private, public trust or community owned.
Concentration of ownership can reduce diversity.
A dual product market means selling content to audiences and audiences to advertisers.
High first-copy costs are typical of media goods.
Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.
Keeping editorial and commercial decisions apart protects independence.

en.title: Photojournalism
en.short: Exposure, composition, captions and the ethics of images, including editing and AI.

sections.heading: What photojournalism does
sections.text: Photojournalism tells news stories through pictures. A strong news image is accurate, relevant and able to show a moment or a human reaction that words may struggle to convey. Photojournalists usually shoot real events without directing them.

sections.heading: Technical basics
sections.text:
Exposure is the amount of light that reaches the sensor. Three settings control it, known as the exposure triangle. Aperture is the opening of the lens, shown as an f-number. A lower f-number means a wider opening and less depth of field. Shutter speed is the length of time that light is let in. A fast speed freezes action. ISO sets the sensor’s sensitivity, and a high ISO adds visible grain or noise.

These settings work together. Suppose f/8, 1/125 second and ISO 100 give good exposure. If you double ISO to 200, you can halve the light by using 1/250 second, which helps freeze movement.

sections.heading: Composition and captions
sections.text:
The rule of thirds places a subject along lines that divide the frame into thirds. Leading lines draw the eye, and framing can show context. Get close, watch the background, and shoot a range of wide, medium and close shots.

A caption should say who, what, where, when and why, and it should not be guesswork. Spell names correctly, and credit the photographer.

sections.heading: Image ethics
sections.text:
Readers trust news pictures as records. Basic adjustments of brightness and contrast are widely accepted, but adding or removing elements is not. The code of the US National Press Photographers Association and the rules of many news organisations set such limits, and these rules differ. Images generated by AI should not be presented as real news photographs, and they should be labelled.

Publishing images of the dead, of the injured and of children needs careful thought. Ask whether the picture’s news value outweighs the harm to the person and the family. Laws on consent and privacy differ by country.

keyPoints: Aperture, shutter speed and ISO form the exposure triangle.
A lower f-number means a wider opening and less depth of field.
A fast shutter speed freezes action.
A caption should cover who, what, where, when and why.
Adding or removing elements in a news photo is not acceptable.
AI-generated images must not be presented as real news photographs.

en.title: Film and Multimedia
en.short: Film history, the stages of production, film language, documentary and classification rules.

sections.heading: Film as mass communication
sections.text:
Film tells stories through moving images and sound. It reaches audiences through cinemas, television and streaming services. Multimedia combines text, sound, images, video and interaction in one product, such as a web documentary.

The Lumière brothers showed films to a paying audience in Paris in 1895. National industries then grew around the world. FESPACO, a major African film festival, began in Ouagadougou in 1969. Nigeria’s video film industry, known as Nollywood, is often dated from Living in Bondage (1992), although film-making in Nigeria began earlier.

sections.heading: Making a film
sections.text:
Production usually has three stages. Pre-production covers the idea, script, budget, casting and shot plan. Production is the shooting. Post-production covers editing, sound, colour and titles. Distribution then brings the work to audiences.

Film language includes shot size, camera angle, movement, lighting, sound and editing. Editing joins shots to control time and meaning. Continuity editing hides the joins, so that action seems unbroken. Montage joins images to suggest an idea, as Soviet film-makers such as Eisenstein explored in the 1920s.

sections.heading: Documentary and regulation
sections.text:
A documentary works with real people and events. John Grierson described it as the creative treatment of actuality. It still involves many choices, so it is not a neutral record. Film-makers should be honest about staged scenes, and they should seek consent where law or ethics requires it.

Film classification differs by country. Examples include Nigeria’s National Film and Video Censors Board, the UK’s British Board of Film Classification, South Africa’s Film and Publication Board and the Kenya Film Classification Board. Copyright and contracts also matter, because a film’s income depends on control of its distribution rights. Streaming has changed how films are financed and watched, so use dated figures.

keyPoints: Multimedia combines text, sound, images, video and interaction.
The main stages are pre-production, production, post-production and distribution.
Continuity editing hides the joins, and montage joins images to suggest an idea.
A documentary uses real people and events, but it still involves choices.
Film classification bodies and rules differ by country.

en.title: Development Communication
en.short: From modernisation theory to participation, with campaigns, community radio and behaviour change.

sections.heading: Modernisation and diffusion
sections.text:
Development communication uses communication to support social change, such as better health, farming and education. Early work followed the modernisation view. Daniel Lerner (1958) linked media exposure to the spread of modern attitudes. Wilbur Schramm (1964) argued that mass media could help national development.

Everett Rogers’ diffusion of innovations (1962) describes how new ideas spread. Adopters are grouped as innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards. The theory remains useful, for example in farm extension work, though it can blame people for not adopting an idea when the true barrier is cost or access.

sections.heading: Critiques and participation
sections.text:
From the 1970s, critics argued that this approach was top-down and assumed that Western paths were the only route to progress. Dependency scholars linked poverty to global inequality. Rogers himself wrote in 1976 about the passing of the dominant paradigm. UNESCO’s MacBride Report, Many Voices, One World (1980), examined unequal global flows of information.

Paulo Freire’s ideas on dialogue and critical awareness supported participatory communication. In this approach, communities help to define problems and solutions, and they are not only receivers of messages.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.text:
Common tools include community radio, local language programmes, folk media and theatre for development, in which a community explores its problems through drama. Entertainment-education puts useful content into popular drama. South Africa’s Soul City, which began in the 1990s, is a well-known health example.

A good campaign begins with audience research. As an invented example, suppose a team wants to raise child immunisation in a rural district in Ghana. Research may show that the true barrier is clinic hours, not lack of knowledge. A radio advert alone would not solve this, so the team should work with health staff and with trusted local voices.

Define measurable aims, test messages, and evaluate results against a baseline, which is the measurement taken before a campaign begins. Knowledge does not always lead to behaviour change, so social norms and service access matter as well.

keyPoints: Early work linked media to modernisation (Lerner 1958, Schramm 1964).
Rogers’ diffusion of innovations names five groups of adopters.
Critics called the early approach top-down and Western-centred.
Freire’s dialogue supports participatory communication.
The MacBride Report (1980) examined unequal flows of information.
Good campaigns begin with audience research and measure against a baseline.

en.title: Media and Society: Critical Perspectives
en.short: Political economy, cultural studies, the public sphere, representation and mediatization.

sections.heading: Power and political economy
sections.text:
Critical approaches ask who holds power through media, and whose interests are served. The Frankfurt School, notably Adorno and Horkheimer, argued that a culture industry produces standardised goods that encourage conformity. Critics find this view elitist and too dismissive of audiences.

Political economy examines ownership, funding and labour. Herman and Chomsky’s propaganda model (1988) proposes that filters such as ownership, advertising and official sourcing shape US news. Critics argue that it underplays journalists’ independence and is hard to test. Schiller’s cultural imperialism thesis held that flows from powerful nations dominate weaker ones. Later scholars point out that audiences adapt content and that regional producers, such as Nigeria’s film industry, compete and export.

sections.heading: Audiences and culture
sections.text:
Stuart Hall’s encoding and decoding model, from the 1970s, argues that audiences can take a dominant, negotiated or oppositional reading of a text.

Representation research asks how the media portray gender, ethnicity, class, disability and regions. Laura Mulvey’s concept of the male gaze (1975) shaped feminist film theory. Studies of coverage of Africa ask how far foreign reporting relies on images of crisis, and how far African media reproduce similar patterns about their own regions and groups.

sections.heading: Public sphere and mediatization
sections.text:
Jürgen Habermas (1962, English translation 1989) described a public sphere in which citizens debate shared concerns. Critics such as Nancy Fraser note that women and other groups were excluded, and that multiple publics exist. Researchers now ask whether digital platforms widen debate or fragment it.

Mediatization theory, developed by writers such as Hjarvard, Couldry and Hepp, examines how institutions such as politics, religion and sport adapt to media logic over time.

sections.heading: Research questions at this level
sections.text: Master’s work is expected to test a theory, not only describe it. Compare contexts, and ask whether a theory developed in the Global North fits the society you study. Scholars such as Francis Nyamnjoh have examined how ideas of belonging and ethnic identity shape African media. Use dated evidence and consider other explanations.

keyPoints: Political economy studies ownership, funding and labour in media.
Herman and Chomsky’s propaganda model (1988) names filters on US news.
Hall describes dominant, negotiated and oppositional readings.
Habermas’s public sphere is debated, including by Fraser.
Mediatization examines how institutions adapt to media logic.
Test theories from the Global North against your own context.

en.title: Political Communication
en.short: Media, politics and publics: framing, priming, campaigns, polls, elections and harmful speech.

sections.heading: Actors and approaches
sections.text:
Political communication studies how political actors, the media and citizens exchange messages and influence one another.

Blumler and Kavanagh (1999) described three ages in advanced democracies. In the first, strong parties dominated communication. In the second, television became central. In the third, the media became abundant, with greater professional campaigning. A fourth age driven by digital media has since been proposed. These stages may not fit every country.

sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.text:
Iyengar and Kinder (1987) showed priming: issues stressed in news can become the standards by which people judge leaders. Entman (1993) clarified framing, in which a frame defines a problem, gives a cause, makes a moral judgement and suggests a remedy. Bennett’s indexing hypothesis (1990) proposes that the range of views in news tends to follow the range of debate among elites.

Election reporting is often criticised as horse race coverage, because it focuses on who is winning and neglects policy. Polls need careful reporting. Give the sample size, the dates, the margin of error, the method and the sponsor.

sections.heading: Elections and regulation
sections.text:
Rules differ widely. Some countries have rules on equal or fair airtime for candidates, on paid political advertising and on publishing polls near election day. In Nigeria, the Electoral Act and the Broadcasting Code both contain relevant rules. In the UK, broadcasters must meet due impartiality rules. Always check the current law.

Online campaigning raises questions of microtargeting, undisclosed sponsorship and false information. Evidence on persuasion is mixed, so avoid simple claims about a platform’s effect on an election.

sections.heading: Harmful speech
sections.text: Speech can also contribute to violence. The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, in its Media Case (trial judgment 2003, appeal 2007), considered the role of media figures in the 1994 genocide. The case distinguishes protected speech from direct incitement, and this remains a central question. Responses to hate speech must balance safety with free expression, because vague rules can also be used against legitimate criticism.

keyPoints: Political communication studies exchanges among political actors, media and citizens.
Blumler and Kavanagh describe three ages of political communication.
Priming affects the standards by which people judge leaders.
Indexing proposes that news follows the range of elite debate.
Report polls with sample size, dates, margin of error, method and sponsor.
The ICTR Media Case is a key reference on incitement and speech.

en.title: Research Methods in Mass Communication
en.short: Designing media research, with surveys, content analysis, interviews, reliability and ethics.

sections.heading: Designing a study
sections.text:
Good research starts with a clear, answerable question. Review the literature and choose a guiding theory. Quantitative research measures and tests relationships. Qualitative research explores meaning and experience. Mixed methods combine the two.

The method must fit the question. If you want to know what newspapers published, use content analysis. If you want to know what readers believe, use a survey or interviews. If you want to test cause and effect, consider an experiment.

sections.heading: Surveys and sampling
sections.text:
A survey asks a sample of people the same questions. A probability sample gives each person a known chance of selection, which allows estimates about the whole population. A convenience sample, such as an online link shared with friends, does not.

For a simple random sample of 1,000 people and a 50% result, the 95% margin of error is about:
1.96 × √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 1,000) = 1.96 × 0.0158 ≈ 0.031, or ±3.1 percentage points.
Real surveys may have larger errors because of design and non-response.

sections.heading: Content analysis and qualitative methods
sections.text:
Content analysis (Berelson, 1952; Krippendorff) studies messages systematically using a coding scheme. Test intercoder reliability, which shows whether different coders agree. Cohen’s kappa corrects for chance agreement. If observed agreement is 0.80 and expected agreement is 0.50, kappa = (0.80 − 0.50) ÷ (1 − 0.50) = 0.60. Krippendorff recommends about 0.80 for his alpha measure.

In-depth interviews and focus groups explore views and how people talk about media. Ethnography studies practice through observation, such as in a newsroom. Discourse analysis, as in the work of Fairclough and van Dijk, relates language to power. Qualitative rigour depends on clear procedures and evidence that readers can follow.

sections.heading: Ethics and digital data
sections.text: Obtain ethical approval where your institution requires it. Seek informed consent, protect participants, and take special care with children. Public posts can still raise privacy issues. Platform data may be incomplete, and access rules change, so state your limits and your dates of collection.

keyPoints: The research question decides the method.
Only probability samples support estimates about a whole population.
With n = 1,000, the margin of error is about ±3.1 points for a simple random sample.
Content analysis needs a coding scheme and an intercoder reliability test.
Content analysis alone cannot show effects on audiences.
Researchers should seek consent and state their limits and dates.
